Master Thesis

Bridging Forecasting and Inventory Control Simulations Using Neural Networks Under Intermittent Demand.

In progress · Rotterdam School of Management · MSc Supply Chain Management · 2026

Uncertainty makes it difficult to determine when and how much to order in supply chain operations. This problem becomes more complex under intermittent demand, a pattern with long periods of zero demand where occurrences are irregular. This sporadic behavior complicates forecasting, affecting replenishment policies and safety stock levels, especially for spare parts and slow-moving products. This thesis builds on the pioneering Croston's method. Croston's will be evaluated against LightGBM, a more sophisticated approach based on decision trees. The resulting forecasts will serve as inputs to a feed-forward neural network–based inventory policy that learns ordering decisions from demand predictions and system variables. The objective of this study is to minimize total inventory costs: holding + shortage costs. To this end, inventory simulations will be run using the VN2 dataset, designed to test inventory replenishment strategies rather than just forecasting accuracy. This thesis project aims to bridge theory and practice, leveraging good forecasts to an effective ordering policy, assuming the role of an inventory planner within a retail chain.

01 — Motivation

Why this project

My main motivation behind this project is to work on a real challenge in supply chain management. Intermittent demand is one of the hardest patterns to forecast in the field, and VN2 frames it as a real competition that simulates a retail inventory environment, where ordering decisions are tested week by week. That setup brings forecasting close to the operational side, which is what made me want to take it on.

Beyond that, forecast accuracy is often treated as the main goal in demand modeling. However, better forecasts do not always lead to better inventory outcomes. The cost of running a warehouse depends on how predictions feed into ordering decisions. This thesis therefore looks at the gap between forecasting and inventory control, testing whether modern methods combined with a learned ordering policy can actually reduce holding and shortage costs.

02 — The Problem

VN2 Inventory Planning Challenge

The work is built around the VN2 Inventory Planning Challenge, a public dataset from a retail inventory competition (Vandeput, 2025). It is organized at the store-product level with weekly observations, and it was designed to test replenishment strategies rather than forecasting accuracy alone.

599 Store–product pairs
67 Stores
297 Unique products
157 Weeks of history
Weekly ordering cycle

The setup is simple. Orders are placed once a week and arrive after a fixed two-week lead time. As a result, an order placed at the end of week t only becomes available at the start of week t+3. The goal is to minimize total inventory cost, calculated as holding plus shortage cost.

  • Holding cost$0.20 / unit / week (on-hand)
  • Shortage cost$1.00 / unit (lost sale)
  • In-transit goodsno holding cost
  • Decision frequencyweekly
  • Lead time2 weeks (fixed)
03 — Approach

From forecast to ordering decision

Two forecasting methods are compared in this study. The first is Croston, used as the classical baseline. The second is LightGBM, a gradient boosting model based on decision trees (Ke et al., 2017). Both feed into a feed-forward neural network that learns weekly ordering decisions from the current inventory state and the forecast.

Forecast → Policy → Simulation

The network is not a rule decided in advance. Instead, it adjusts its weights through repeated runs of the simulation, gradually moving toward orders that reduce total cost. In this way, the policy can capture behavior that classical rules such as (s,S) or base-stock policies cannot easily represent. Click on Model Selection for more details on the forecasting methods used in this study.

04 — Exploratory Data Analysis

A first look at the data

The three raw files (sales, in-stock, initial state) were joined and reshaped to long format. From there, a key derived variable was computed: actual_demand = sales + missed_sales. This correction matters because raw sales understate true demand whenever a stockout occurs, and removing that bias is essential for any forecasting work.

Demand classification

Each of the 599 store-product series was classified using the Syntetos-Boylan scheme, which segments demand into four categories based on the Average Demand Interval (ADI) and the squared Coefficient of Variation (CV²). The result confirms that this dataset is dominated by sparse demand.

About 85% of SKUs fall into the intermittent or lumpy categories, which means most products show long stretches of zero demand. In addition, 18% of products are classified differently across stores, so the same product can be smooth in one store and lumpy in another.

Temporal patterns

Two clear temporal patterns emerged. First, a recurring year-end demand spike around weeks 50-51, present in every complete year of the dataset. Second, a mild upward trend over the full period, confirmed by the Mann-Kendall test (τ = 0.35, p < 0.001). Both patterns violate Croston's stationarity assumption and motivate LightGBM, which can absorb seasonality and trend through temporal covariates.

Zero-demand and stockouts

The median SKU shows zero demand in 46.5% of weeks, so sparse demand is the norm rather than the exception. When zero-demand rate is plotted against stockout rate per SKU, four distinct populations appear, separating genuine demand absence from supply-driven zeros. This distinction matters because stockouts make observed sales understate true demand, and ignoring it would bias both forecasting and policy evaluation.

05 — Forecast target

What is being tried to forecast?

The forecast target is simple. Each week, given everything observed up to week t, the model predicts actual_demand for the next two weeks, t+1 and t+2. Those two numbers feed directly into the ordering rule and decide how much stock to order.

06 — Model Selection

Croston's method (classical baseline)

John D. Croston introduced the first forecasting method specifically designed for intermittent demand (Croston, 1972). The core idea is to split the demand series into two pieces: the size of demand when it actually occurs, and the number of periods between one demand event and the next. Each piece is then smoothed independently using simple exponential smoothing. The final forecast is the smoothed size divided by the smoothed interval.

When demand occurs at time t (yt > 0):

zt = α yt + (1 − α) zt−1
pt = α qt + (1 − α) pt−1

When no demand at time t (yt = 0):

zt = zt−1 ,    pt = pt−1

Forecast for h periods ahead:

ŷt+h = zt / pt
α
smoothing parameter, 0 < α ≤ 1 (typically 0.1–0.3).
yt
observed demand at time t.
zt
smoothed estimate of demand size.
pt
smoothed estimate of the inter-arrival interval.
qt
number of periods since the previous non-zero demand.
Adapted from Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice (2nd ed.), §12.2. Original method: Croston, J. D. (1972), Operational Research Quarterly, 23(3), 289–303.

Why Croston as the baseline

Croston is a univariate method. It uses only past demand to forecast future demand and cannot include covariates such as price, promotions, calendar effects, or stock availability, even though these are often the real drivers of intermittent demand. That is the main reason a second model, LightGBM, is included in the comparison.

LightGBM (modern alternative)

LightGBM is a gradient boosting framework developed at Microsoft Research (Ke et al., 2017). It belongs to a wider family known as gradient boosting machines (GBMs), introduced by Jerome Friedman in 2001. Unlike Croston, LightGBM can use covariates, learn from many series at once, and adapt to seasonality and trend.

The core idea behind gradient boosting is additive learning. Instead of fitting one complex model, a GBM builds many simple models, usually small decision trees, and adds their predictions together. The first tree predicts the target as best it can. Each new tree then focuses on the mistakes the previous trees made, called the residuals. Adding the new tree's prediction to the running total brings the combined forecast closer to the truth, step by step.

Each tree corrects the errors of the previous ones

LightGBM is a specific implementation of this idea, optimized for speed and scale (Ke et al., 2017). Traditional gradient boosting can be slow because it considers every data point and every feature at every split. LightGBM solves this through two main tricks. Leaf-wise tree growth picks the most useful split at each step rather than expanding the tree uniformly. Histogram-based binning groups continuous values into bins, which makes split finding much faster. For a problem with hundreds of series and many features, those tricks are what make the approach feasible at all.

Beyond inventory forecasting, LightGBM is used widely across machine learning: search ranking (it was originally developed for ranking tasks at Microsoft), credit scoring and fraud detection, click-through-rate prediction, recommendation systems, and many tabular regression and classification problems. The Python package lightgbm is the standard interface, installed with pip install lightgbm.

At each boosting step m:

Fm(x) = Fm−1(x) + γ · fm(x)

Final forecast after M trees:

ŷ(x) = FM(x)
Fm(x)
combined prediction after m boosting rounds.
fm(x)
the m-th decision tree, fit to the gradient of the loss with respect to Fm−1.
γ
learning rate (shrinkage), typically 0.05–0.1.
M
total number of trees in the ensemble.
Adapted from Friedman, J. H. (2001), Greedy function approximation, and the LightGBM documentation.

Why LightGBM fits intermittent demand

Three properties make LightGBM well suited to this problem. First, it can include covariates such as store ID, product ID, week-of-year, lagged demand, and stock availability, all of which can explain when demand occurs. Second, it learns from all 599 store-product series at once rather than treating each in isolation, which lets it borrow strength across SKUs that behave similarly. Third, it can be configured to handle the high share of zeros typical in intermittent demand through specialized loss functions.

Recent studies confirm the advantage in practice. Anderer and Li (2021) report 25 to 40 percent MASE improvements over Croston variants on automotive spare parts. Seeger et al. (2025) report comparable gains across retail (including VN2), automotive, and aerospace datasets.

VN2 in practice

The first VN2 Inventory Planning Competition (October–November 2025, 183 participants) confirmed LightGBM's relevance for this exact problem. In his post-competition retrospective, the host Nicolas Vandeput ranked LightGBM as A-tier among forecasting approaches, noting it was still among the top solutions and remains his own preferred model. Forecasting models used by the top 10 finishers:

Across the full top 20, 9 finishers used LightGBM in some form, more than any other forecasting tool. CatBoost, a sibling gradient-boosting framework, was used by 3 additional participants, bringing the share of gradient-boosting approaches to 12 out of 20 (60%). The remaining methods include deep learning models (DeepAR, NBEATS, NHiTS, Chronos), classical statistical methods (exponential smoothing, ARIMA, moving averages), and bespoke ensembles.

07 — Ordering policy

From forecast to order: the bridge

A forecast tells you what demand will probably be; it doesn't tell you how much to order. The ordering policy is the function that turns the forecast and the current inventory state into an order quantity each week. Both Croston and LightGBM produce mean (point) forecasts for the next two weeks, so risk is handled at the policy stage, not baked into the forecast. This thesis compares a classical base-stock policy as the baseline against a feed-forward neural network that learns the policy from simulation.

The neural network policy connects forecast and state to the order quantity

Baseline: base-stock policy

A base-stock policy is a classical inventory rule. It defines a target stock level (typically the forecast over the lead time plus a safety buffer), then orders the difference between that target and the current inventory position. It is simple, interpretable, and easy to tune, which makes it a fair benchmark for any learned approach to beat.

The learned policy: feed-forward neural network

A feed-forward neural network is a stack of layers. Each layer computes a linear combination of the previous layer's outputs and passes the result through a non-linear activation function. Stacking these layers lets the network approximate complex mappings from inputs to outputs.

The hidden layers in this policy use ReLU (rectified linear unit), defined as f(x) = max(0, x). ReLU fits this problem for three reasons: it is cheap to compute, it does not saturate for positive values (so gradients flow during training), and it naturally enforces non-negativity in intermediate features, a useful inductive bias when modeling non-negative quantities like demand and inventory.

Feed-forward network: inputs → ReLU hidden layer → order quantity

The weekly loop

The simulation runs for 8 weeks: 2 initialization weeks and 6 measured weeks. Each week, the model forecasts demand, the policy chooses an order, demand realizes, and a holding plus shortage cost is recorded. Because orders take 2 weeks to arrive, the first 2 weeks are a warm-up where orders placed only land later. The total cost over the 6 measured weeks is the score for the policy.

8 weekly cycles: 2 initialization weeks (warm-up due to lead time), 6 measured weeks

Why a learned policy

A neural network policy uses inventory state and forecast jointly rather than committing to a safety margin in advance. It adapts to the asymmetric cost of shortages versus overstocks. And it improves directly through the simulation environment used to evaluate it.
